---
title: "Scales and guides"
description: >
  How data values become colour, size, shape, opacity, line type, and axis
  positions. Continuous, discrete, binned, manual, gradient, date/time, and
  identity scales, limit shortcuts, trained domains, and controlling the legends
  they produce.
---

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.retina = 2,
  out.width = "100%",
  eval = requireNamespace("vellumplot", quietly = TRUE)
)
library(vellumplot)
```

A *scale* is the function that turns a data value into something you can see: a
colour, a marker size, a shape, or a position along an axis. In vellumplot every
mapped encoding gets a scale automatically, trained from the data, so most
plots need no explicit scale at all. You reach for a `scale_*()` call only when
you want to override the default: change the palette, set a transform, fix the
limits, or rename the guide.

The key idea is *training*. When you map `color = hp`, vellumplot scans the `hp`
values across every layer, works out the domain, and builds a continuous colour
scale with a legend. Add a `scale_*()` and you are declaring an override on top
of that trained default, not replacing the whole machine.

## Colour, continuous and discrete

Continuous data get a smooth colour ramp; discrete data get a categorical
palette. The `palette` argument takes a vector of colours or a single palette
name passed to `grDevices::hcl.colors()` (for example `"Batlow"`, `"Blues"`,
`"Set 2"`).

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp, size = 3) |>
  scale_color_continuous(palette = "Viridis", name = "Horsepower")
```

For a two-colour ramp, `scale_color_gradient()` takes the endpoints directly, and
`scale_color_gradientn()` an arbitrary n-stop ramp. If you are coming from
ggplot2, the familiar named constructors are here too and are simply wrappers
over `palette =`: `scale_color_viridis_c()` / `_d()` for the viridis maps,
`scale_color_brewer()` (discrete) / `scale_color_distiller()` (continuous) for
ColorBrewer-style palettes. Set `limits =` on a continuous colour scale to fix
its mapped range. The rest of ggplot2's colour constructors are here as well,
with ggplot2's argument names: `scale_color_hue()`, `scale_color_grey()` and
`scale_color_ordinal()` for categories, and the binned `scale_color_steps()`,
`scale_color_steps2()`, `scale_color_stepsn()`, `scale_color_fermenter()` and
`scale_color_viridis_b()`. Each has its `colour` and `fill` spellings.

For categories, `scale_color_manual()` maps levels to colours; naming the
values pins each level to a specific colour.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl), size = 3) |>
  scale_color_manual(values = c("4" = "#1b9e77", "6" = "#d95f02", "8" = "#7570b3"))
```

For signed or anomaly data — where a value like zero is meaningfully neutral —
`scale_color_gradient2()` (and `scale_fill_gradient2()`) draw a diverging ramp
around a `midpoint`. It rescales *about* the midpoint, so the neutral `mid`
colour always lands on that value even when the data range is lopsided:

```{r}
anom <- data.frame(x = 1:20, y = 1:20, resid = seq(-3, 6, length.out = 20))
vplot(anom) |>
  mark_point(x = x, y = y, color = resid, size = 3) |>
  scale_color_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey90", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0)
```

Ramps built from a plain colour vector — a `scale_color_gradient(low, high)`, or a
`palette` given as colours — are interpolated in the perceptually-uniform **Oklab**
space, not sRGB, so the ramp and its colourbar read evenly instead of dipping
through a muddy, over-dark middle (a blue→yellow ramp no longer passes through
grey). Designed perceptual palettes such as the default `Batlow` or any
`hcl.colors()` name are already uniform and unchanged. To blend in sRGB (or CIE
Lab) instead, set `options(vellumplot.color.interpolation = "srgb")` (or `"lab"`).
A gradient *fill* opts in per gradient with
`linear_gradient(..., interpolation = "oklab")`.

## Binned colour

`scale_fill_binned()` and `scale_color_binned()` cut a continuous aesthetic
into classes and give it a discrete legend, which is what you want for a
choropleth or a heatmap you read by band rather than by exact value. Choose the
classification `style` (`"quantile"`, `"equal"`, `"pretty"`, or any
`classInt::classIntervals()` style) and the number of classes `n`.

```{r}
grid <- expand.grid(x = 1:10, y = 1:10)
grid$z <- with(grid, x * y)
vplot(grid) |>
  mark_tile(x = x, y = y, fill = z) |>
  scale_fill_binned(style = "quantile", n = 5, palette = "Mako")
```

## Two variables on one colour

A bivariate map colours each feature by two variables at once. `bi_class()`
bins both over the whole table and writes one `"x-y"` class column; map a fill
or colour to it and the scale and its 2-D legend follow. The legend is a grid
of swatches, the first variable along the bottom and the second up the side,
and each edge is labelled with the class breaks `bi_class()` chose, so you can
read which range a colour stands for.

```{r}
d <- bi_class(mtcars, hp, wt)
vplot(d) |>
  mark_point(x = hp, y = wt, color = bi_class, size = 3) |>
  scale_color_bivariate(palette = "GrPink", xlab = "Power", ylab = "Weight")
```

`guide_bivariate(rotate = TRUE)` turns the grid 45 degrees into a diamond, with
low-low at the bottom and high-high at the top, the form many bivariate maps
use. `labels = FALSE` drops the break labels.

```{r}
vplot(d) |>
  mark_point(x = hp, y = wt, color = bi_class, size = 3) |>
  guides(color = guide_bivariate(rotate = TRUE))
```

## Size, shape, and edge width

Non-colour aesthetics have scales too. `scale_size()` maps values linearly to a
marker-size `range` (in mm); `scale_shape()` cycles a set of shapes over the
levels of a discrete aesthetic; `scale_edge_width()` does for network edges
what `scale_size()` does for points.

The shape palette is `"circle"`, `"square"`, `"triangle"`, `"diamond"`, `"plus"`,
`"cross"`, `"triangle_down"`, and `"star"` — eight in all, so a mapped `shape`
covers up to eight levels automatically. Pass a subset (or a reordering) with
`scale_shape(values = ...)`. Filled shapes take the mark's `fill`/`color`, so an
open marker is `fill = NA` with a `color`.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, size = hp, color = factor(cyl)) |>
  scale_size(range = c(2, 9), name = "hp")
```

`scale_size()` maps the value to the marker's *radius*. For bubble charts prefer
`scale_size_area()`, which maps to the *area* (value 0 → size 0) so the ink is
proportional to the value — the honest encoding:

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, size = hp) |>
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10)
```

The other ggplot2 size constructors work too: `scale_radius()`,
`scale_size_continuous()`, `scale_size_binned()` (sizes by class, see
`guide_bins()` below), `scale_size_discrete()` / `scale_size_ordinal()` and
`scale_size_manual()`. The shape, line-type and alpha scales have their
`_manual()` and `_discrete()` forms, and `scale_shape_manual()` and
`scale_linetype_manual()` also take ggplot2's numeric codes as `values`.

A discrete scale drops the factor levels no row uses, as in ggplot2.
`drop = FALSE` keeps them in the legend and in the palette, so a level keeps its
key even when it is absent from this subset of the data. It works on every
discrete scale: colour, fill, shape, line type, size and alpha.

```{r}
cars6 <- subset(mtcars, cyl != 6)
cars6$cyl <- factor(cars6$cyl, levels = c(4, 6, 8), ordered = TRUE)
vplot(cars6) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, size = cyl) |>
  scale_size_discrete(drop = FALSE)
```

## Line width

`linewidth` is a mapped aesthetic on `mark_line()`, `mark_step()` and
`mark_segment()`: `scale_linewidth()` rescales the data onto a width `range` in
`lwd` units, and draws its own legend.

```{r}
vplot(pressure) |>
  mark_line(x = temperature, y = pressure, linewidth = pressure) |>
  scale_linewidth(range = c(0.5, 6))
```

Each series is drawn as one stroke whose width varies smoothly between the
values at its vertices, so the line tapers instead of stepping, and it stays a
single element in SVG and PDF. A few cases fall back to drawing each segment at
one width, the mean of its two endpoint values: a continuous `color` mapped on
the same line (each segment keeps its own colour), a dashed or dotted
`linetype`, a sketch theme, and a missing width.

Network edges keep their own scale: a mapped `linewidth` on `mark_edges()`
trains `scale_edge_width()`, independently of `scale_linewidth()`, so one plot
can map edge width and line width to different variables.

## Opacity and line type

`alpha` and `linetype` are mapped aesthetics too. `scale_alpha()` maps a
continuous variable to opacity (its `range` defaults to `c(0.1, 1)`), a good way
to let density show through an overplotted cloud.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, alpha = hp, size = 3) |>
  scale_alpha(range = c(0.2, 1))
```

`scale_linetype()` maps a discrete variable to line types, cycling `"solid"`,
`"dashed"`, `"dotted"`, and so on. It applies to line-like marks
(`mark_line()`, `mark_step()`).

```{r}
series <- data.frame(
  x = rep(1:20, 3),
  y = c(cumsum(rnorm(20)), cumsum(rnorm(20)), cumsum(rnorm(20))),
  series = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), each = 20)
)
vplot(series) |>
  mark_line(x = x, y = y, linetype = series)
```

## Identity scales

Sometimes a column *already* holds the exact aesthetic values you want: actual
colour names, sizes in millimetres, shape names. An identity scale uses them
verbatim and draws no legend. There is a variant for each aesthetic:
`scale_color_identity()`, `scale_fill_identity()`, `scale_size_identity()`,
`scale_shape_identity()`, `scale_alpha_identity()`, `scale_linetype_identity()`.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(
  x = 1:5, y = 1:5,
  col = c("firebrick", "goldenrod", "forestgreen", "steelblue", "purple")
)
vplot(df) |>
  mark_point(x = x, y = y, color = col, size = 6) |>
  scale_color_identity()
```

## Position scales

`scale_x_continuous()` and `scale_y_continuous()` control the axes. By default
they train from the data with a small expansion; override them to set `limits`,
apply a `trans` (`"log10"`, `"sqrt"`, `"symlog"`, `"reverse"`), or supply
explicit `breaks` and `labels`. Categorical axes use `scale_x_discrete()` and
`scale_y_discrete()`, whose `limits` set the order or subset of levels.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(10, 35), breaks = seq(10, 35, 5)) |>
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10", name = "Weight (log scale)")
```

Where `"log10"` cannot go — data that crosses zero or spans positive and negative
values over several orders of magnitude — `"symlog"` gives a symmetric-log axis:
linear through zero, logarithmic in each tail, with ticks at zero and signed
powers of ten.

```{r}
signed <- data.frame(v = c(-1000, -100, -10, 0, 10, 100, 1000), y = 1:7)
vplot(signed) |>
  mark_point(x = v, y = y) |>
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "symlog")
```

To set limits without spelling out a whole scale, use the shortcuts `xlim()`,
`ylim()`, and `lims()` (the last takes one named argument per aesthetic):

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  lims(x = c(0, 6), y = c(0, 40))
```

### Scale transform vs display transform

A `scale_*(trans=)` (above) transforms the *data*: it picks its breaks in the
transformed space, so a `"log10"` axis is labelled `1, 10, 100`. `coord_trans()`
instead warps only the *display*, after the scale has trained — the breaks stay at
their original data values, so the axis keeps those labels but they sit at warped
positions (gridlines bunch up, and straight lines curve). Use it to show data on a
log display without relabelling the axis in powers of ten:

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  mark_line(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  coord_trans(y = "log10")
```

Each of `x` / `y` takes a transform name (`"log10"`, `"sqrt"`, `"identity"`) or a
`scales::transform_*()` object. It applies to the common marks (points, lines,
areas, bars, tiles, smooths, text); interval/segment, boxplot, and raster marks
are not warped yet.

### Secondary axes

A secondary axis adds a second set of ticks and labels on the opposite edge (top
for `x`, right for `y`), computed as a 1:1 monotonic transform of the primary
axis. Pass `sec_axis()` to the `sec.axis` argument of a continuous position
scale. The classic use is a unit conversion — plot in Celsius, label the top in
Fahrenheit:

```{r}
vplot(data.frame(celsius = 0:100, y = (0:100)^2)) |>
  mark_line(x = celsius, y = y) |>
  scale_x_continuous(name = "°C", sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . * 1.8 + 32, name = "°F"))
```

`dup_axis()` is the identity special case — it simply duplicates the axis on the
far edge, handy for reading a wide plot from either side:

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  scale_y_continuous(sec.axis = dup_axis())
```

The transform can be a formula (`~ . * 2`), a function, or a
`scales::transform_*()` object, and must be monotonic. This is a labelling
convenience, *not* an independent second axis with its own data. It is currently
supported on continuous position scales under the default Cartesian coordinate
system, with shared scales across facets; combining it with `coord_flip()` /
`coord_polar()` / `coord_trans()`, with free facet scales, or with
`add_marginal()` raises an error, and in a plot composition the secondary axis is
not drawn.

## Date and time axes

A `Date` or `POSIXct` column gets a date axis automatically. To control the
break interval or the label format, declare `scale_x_date()` (or
`scale_x_datetime()` / `scale_x_time()`): `date_breaks` takes an interval string
like `"6 months"`, and `date_labels` a `strftime()` format.

```{r}
econ <- data.frame(
  day = as.Date("2020-01-01") + 0:729,
  value = cumsum(rnorm(730))
)
vplot(econ) |>
  mark_line(x = day, y = value) |>
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y")
```

## Axis guides

The axis of a position scale is a guide too. `guide_axis()` is the tool for
crowded labels. `n.dodge = 2` staggers them over two rows, `angle` rotates
them, and `check.overlap = TRUE` drops the ones that would collide. The label
gutter is measured with the dodging and rotation, so nothing is clipped. Pass
it through `guides(x = )` / `guides(y = )` or a scale's `guide =` argument.

```{r}
states <- data.frame(state = state.name[1:12], area = state.area[1:12] / 1000)
vplot(states) |>
  mark_bar(x = state, y = area) |>
  guides(x = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2))
```

`minor.ticks = TRUE` adds short ticks between the breaks, and `cap` ends the
axis line at the outermost breaks instead of running it along the whole panel
(it needs a theme that draws an axis line, such as `theme_classic()`).
`guide_axis_logticks()` draws long, middle and short ticks on a log10 axis, and
`guides(x = "none")` keeps the axis but drops its labels and ticks.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  theme_classic() |>
  guides(x = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE, cap = "both"), y = guide_axis(cap = "both"))
```

The date, date-time and time scales and the binned position scales
(`scale_x_binned()`) take `guide =` as well. Breaks chosen with `date_breaks`
are fitted to the guide, so a staggered or rotated axis gets denser breaks:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
months <- data.frame(day = as.Date("2024-01-01") + 0:365, value = cumsum(rnorm(366)))
vplot(months) |>
  mark_line(x = day, y = value) |>
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y", guide = guide_axis(angle = 45))
```

## Guides come for free

Every scale that needs a legend produces one, and vellumplot stacks multiple
legends automatically. Map two aesthetics and you get two guides without asking.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp, size = disp) |>
  scale_color_continuous(palette = "Batlow", name = "Horsepower") |>
  scale_size(range = c(1, 8), name = "Displacement")
```

## Controlling a legend

`guides()` overrides a single legend without respelling its scale. Pass
`"none"` to hide it, or `guide_legend()` to reverse the key order or override
the title.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl)) |>
  guides(color = guide_legend(title = "Cylinders", reverse = TRUE))
```

Hiding a legend keeps the mapping; the marks stay coloured, only the guide
disappears:

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl)) |>
  guides(color = "none")
```

Every legend guide takes `position =` (`"right"`, `"left"`, `"top"`,
`"bottom"` or `"inside"`), which overrides `theme(legend.position = )` for that
one legend, as in ggplot2 3.5. Legends can then sit on different sides of one
plot; a legend at the top or bottom is laid out horizontally.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl), size = hp) |>
  guides(color = guide_legend(position = "bottom"))
```

`override.aes` styles the legend **keys** independently of the data --- the fix
for a scatter of small, translucent points whose keys you still want big and
readable. Pass a named list of aesthetics (`size`, `alpha`, `colour`, `fill`,
`shape`, `linewidth`); only the swatches change, never the marks.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl), alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) |>
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5, alpha = 1)))
```

For a *continuous* colour scale the guide is a colour bar. `guide_colourbar()`
sizes it (`barwidth` / `barheight`, in mm), toggles the break `ticks` (and their
colour), and moves the labels to the left of the bar.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp) |>
  guides(color = guide_colourbar(
    barwidth = 8, barheight = 60, ticks = FALSE, label.position = "left"
  ))
```

A *binned* colour scale draws as discrete swatches by default;
`guide_coloursteps()` renders it as a segmented bar instead, labelled at the bin
boundaries (and it takes the same `barwidth` / `barheight` / `ticks` tunables).

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp) |>
  scale_color_binned() |>
  guides(color = guide_coloursteps())
```

`guide_bins()` is ggplot2's legend for a binned scale: one key per bin, stacked
edge to edge, with the bin boundaries on a small axis beside them rather than
an interval label on each key. `show.limits = TRUE` also labels the outer
limits. It works on `scale_size_binned()` and the binned colour scales.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, size = hp) |>
  scale_size_binned() |>
  guides(size = guide_bins(show.limits = TRUE))
```

A *size* legend defaults to stacked keys; `guide_legend(nested = TRUE)` draws it
as a proportional-symbol legend --- concentric circles sharing a baseline, each
with a leader to its label. It reads size directly and is compact, and suits a
wide size range so the circles are large enough to tell apart.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, size = hp) |>
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) |>
  guides(size = guide_legend(nested = TRUE))
```

### Colour and fill together

`color` and `fill` are separate scales, each with its own legend, so a plot can
map outline and interior to different variables and style them independently.
When both show the same variable under the same title, their legends merge into
one: each key is filled by the fill scale and outlined by the colour scale.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(
    x = wt, y = mpg, fill = factor(cyl), color = factor(cyl),
    shape = "circle filled", size = 3
  ) |>
  scale_color_manual(values = c("4" = "#1b9e77", "6" = "#d95f02", "8" = "#7570b3")) |>
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("4" = "#b3e2cd", "6" = "#fdcdac", "8" = "#cbd5e8")) |>
  labs(color = "Cylinders", fill = "Cylinders")
```

Give the two a different title, or map different variables, and you get two
legends. `labs(fill =)`, `guides(fill =)` and `lims(fill =)` address the fill
scale alone.

## Rich titles

Any scale `name` (and any `labs()` title) accepts `md()`, a small markdown
subset for bold, italic, superscript, subscript, and coloured spans. Handy for
units and formulae.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp) |>
  scale_color_continuous(name = md("Power (hp m^2^)"))
```

### Math in a plot

For real formulae, `tex()` takes TeX notation and `plotmath()` R's plotmath
notation (what ggplot2 reads with `parse = TRUE`); `md()` labels take inline
math between `$` signs. vellum typesets the math itself, the same in PNG, SVG,
PDF and the widget. A math label goes in every title, a discrete legend's
`labels =` (a list, one label per key), `mark_text()` / `mark_label()`
(`parse = TRUE` reads a column as plotmath), `annotate()`, and the facet
strips through `label_parsed`. Alt text and tooltips show the TeX source.

```{r}
#| fig.height: 4
d <- data.frame(
  x = rep(1:5, 2),
  y = c(1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9),
  g = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 5),
  f = rep(c("alpha == 0.5", "beta[2]"), each = 5),
  lab = c("x^2", "hat(y)", "frac(1, n)", "bar(x)", "sqrt(z)")
)
vplot(d) |>
  mark_line(x = x, y = y, color = g) |>
  mark_text(x = x, y = y, label = lab, parse = TRUE, nudge_y = 4) |>
  facet_wrap(~f, labeller = label_parsed) |>
  scale_color_discrete(labels = list(tex("e^{x}"), tex("2x - 1"))) |>
  labs(
    title = md("Growth with rate $\\lambda$ per **step**"),
    x = tex("t\\ (\\mathrm{s})"),
    y = plotmath("hat(N)[t]")
  )
```

Faceted plots add one more question: should panels share a scale or train their
own? That is the `resolve_scale()` lattice, covered in
**[Facets and composition](facets-and-composition.html)**. For stat-derived
aesthetics like `after_stat(count)`, see
**[Statistical marks](statistical-marks.html)**.
